title: Giant sea spiders emit eerie glow deep below the ocean waves
content: *Eight_long_sea_spider_legs_glow_blue_in_the_dark
This eerie glow was seen coming from the long legs of one of the largest species of giant sea spiders (Colossendeis tasmanica). The critter haunts an abyss off Australia.
Deep in the dark Australian Abyss, what’s visible can be scarier than the unseen. There, giant sea spiders scuttle along like glowing ghosts.

The critters are not true spiders but relatives that split off from a common ancestor on the arthropod family tree some 500 million years ago. Researchers have just described the sea spiders’ glow in the October Deep Sea Research Part I: Oceanographic Research Papers.
“It’s quite impressive for people scared of spiders,” says Jérôme Mallefet. The marine biologist works for the Catholic University of Louvain in Belgium.
His team’s photos confirm that these creatures can emit light. Some 76 percent of deep-sea creatures produce a clear glow. Known as bioluminescence, this trait dates back 540 million years.
iFhttps://www.sciencenews.org/conversion/zephr-iframe-test

Mallefet and his colleagues discovered the sea spiders on a 2017 expedition. They had been surveying part of a deep-sea trench off southeastern Australia. The team hauled up 25,000 specimens in nets. The critters had been retrieved from nearly 5,000 meters (more than 3 miles) below the surface.

Aboard the RV Investigator, Mallefet tested these deep-sea creatures for bioluminescence. “I spent most of my time in a dark cold room,” Mallefet recalls. “I believe I was a little bit crazy, but I like that.”

Poking the biggest of the sea spiders (Colossendeis tasmanica) raised a dim light. But adding potassium chloride, a type of salt, can excite bioluminescent cells. The chemical triggered them to glow brightly for up to 10 minutes. Another giant sea spider, C. minor, also shone on its own.
*This_orange-yellow_giant_sea_spider_sports_eight_long_legs_and_a_body_the_size_of_a_person's_finger

fCThough it has roughly a finger-sized body, C. tasmanica’s legs can stretch out as much as 25 centimeters (10 inches). Those legs don’t glow all the time. They seem to first need some type of trigger.
All living creatures emit a weak glow. That’s different from the bright light coming from these stimulated sea spiders.

The images Mallefet’s team took support past reports of glowing sea spiders. One report from more than a century ago was especially poetic: “The creature, as it lay on its back, shone like a star, all its legs being lit along their surface with a strange blue radiance.”
Giant sea spiders’ legs contain the digestive tract, Mallefet says. That means these animals might get their glow from the creatures they eat — such as sea anemones, his team suggests.

Three sea-spider species glowed green when Mallefet shone ultraviolet and blue light on them. Glowing in response to certain wavelengths of light is called fluorescence. Several amphibians and even platypuses gleam the same way, too.

Mallefet isn’t sure what value sea spiders get from fluorescing. He suspects their glow might attract mates. Or, since the glow is in their legs, maybe these critters use them as a searchlight for seafloor prey.

Once the critters spot something tasty, the sea spiders might collapse their legs down, grabbing their victim. Then a needlelike part of their proboscis — a tube-like mouth structure — might stab into their prey, liquefying its tissues before sucking it up. Confirming that would take deep-sea video with next-level imaging.

title: Farm plants may help fight infections, teen finds
content: *a_teen_girl_smiles_in_front_of_a_project_poster_titled_'field_of_dreams'_on_a_background_of_flowerin
Locklyn Ward, 14, investigated whether two dozen plants found on her family’s farm could help fight bacterial infections.

Locklyn Ward, 14, lives on a farm in Oklahoma. One evening while she was helping feed the cows, she got curious about the plants growing in the field. She knew that scientists are always searching for new ways to fight infections. So she set out to see if any of the plants growing on her family’s farm could take down bacteria.

Locklyn picked 24 plants; 12 were native to her state. She cut the plants into one-gram (four hundredths of an ounce) pieces and boiled each to extract chemicals from it. Then, she tested those extracts against two types of bacteria: Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus epidermidis. Locklyn also tested antibiotics that are currently used to treat infections.
*a_teen_girl_smiles_standing_in_front_of_a_pool_on_a_sunny_day
fCAs a member of the Cherokee Nation, Locklyn has always been interested in local plants’ traditional and medicinal uses.

The test involved paper disks soaked in either the plant extracts or current antibiotics. Locklyn placed those soaked disks into dishes containing bacteria. If chemicals from the farm plants had antibiotic powers, the bacteria around those paper disks would die.

No farm-plant extract worked as well as current medicines. But 13 of the 24 plants did kill some bacteria. These included seven native plants. Locklyn hopes her results may point to new ways to fight germs. Overuse of current antibiotics is leading to more drug-resistant bacteria, so new solutions are much needed.

Locklyn did this project as an eighth grader at Grove Middle School in Grove, Okla. Her research earned her a finalist spot in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge. This program is run by Society for Science, which also publishes Science News Explores. Here, Locklyn shares science-fair experiences and advice.

“Growing up, my grandmother often talked with me about how plants and herbs can be used for medicine and healing,” Locklyn says. “And as a citizen of the Cherokee Nation, I’ve always been interested in learning more about plants and their traditional and potential medicinal uses.”

“Managing my time, because I’m involved in many extracurriculars,” Locklyn says. With church activities and sports, her schedule is a bit chaotic, she says. Doing research required finding pockets of time on weekends and after school — and sometimes saying no to other fun plans. “I used Google Calendar,” she says. “That helped a lot.”

Locklyn’s science-fair teacher was a huge help. “She’s the one if I got bad results, she’d be like, ‘It’s okay, Locklyn, just keep going. You’re gonna get it.’” She was “very inspirational to me,” the teen says. “She’s the best.” Locklyn’s biggest piece of advice for science fair newbies is to find a mentor like this to help stay motivated through times of struggle and stress.

title: Scientists Say: Sanguivore
content: *a_vampire_bat_runs_across_dark_ground
Vampire bats, such as Desmodus rotundus, evolved limbs that allow them to run and jump with great agility. When seeking a blood meal, these bats may sprint after prey or creep up on sleeping animals.

iFhttps://w.soundcloud.com/player/?url=https%3A//api.soundcloud.com/tracks/soundcloud%253Atracks%253A2426110491&color=%23ff5500&auto_play=false&hide_related=false&show_comments=true&show_user=true&show_reposts=false&show_teaser=true
A sanguivore is an animal that eats blood.
Some species survive on blood alone. They are called obligate sanguivores. Bedbugs, ticks and vampire bats are examples.
Other species drink blood to supplement their diet. Or they drink blood only at certain stages of their life. Part-time blood drinkers are called facultative sanguivores.
Consider mosquitoes. They usually eat plant nectar. But female mosquitoes need the protein in blood to help them mature their eggs.

Oxpeckers are another example of part-time vampires. These birds perch atop grazing rhinos and zebras in the African savannah and pluck ticks from the animals’ hides. They also lap up blood at the wound site where the tick was. Sometimes these birds pick open old wounds on the animal’s hide for an extra blood snack.

Blood doesn’t have many nutrients and packs few calories. It consists mostly of water. Most foods contain easy-to-digest sugars and fats. But blood doesn’t contain much of either. Instead, most of blood’s calories come from proteins, which are harder to digest. Blood also comes loaded with iron. Animals need some iron in their diet. But the high levels found in blood can be toxic.

Animals that eat blood must handle these dietary challenges. Take vampire bats. The three species of them are the only known mammals that are obligate sanguivores. Specialized kidneys let vampire bats purge water quickly. In fact, they usually begin peeing while they eat. Their digestive systems absorb very little iron from their food. And their guts also host microbes that help them break down blood proteins. These microbes also create vitamins that the bats cannot get from blood.
The poor nutritional quality of blood probably explains why humans never evolved to drink it.

title: These 5 quirks reveal how AI doesn’t think like we do
content: *an_illustration_of_a_complicated_Rube_Goldberg_machine

A Rube Goldberg machine uses a dizzyingly complex process to accomplish a simple task. Similarly, instead of learning simple concepts, AI’s large language models follow convoluted and complicated paths to arrive at an answer.
Hold a pen horizontally with both hands, then let go of one side. What happens?

YouTuber FatherPhi challenged chatbots with this question. ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok all agreed that the unsupported end will rotate downward. FatherPhi then showed each chatbot a live demonstration. After releasing one end of a pen, he easily held it out horizontally with only his other hand.
“What just happened?” he asked ChatGPT.
“I saw the pen rotate exactly as expected,” the bot answered.
iFhttps://www.youtube.com/embed/gPthZLTnzu8?feature=oembed
“I saw the pen rotate exactly as expected,” says ChatGPT. That was its response to a pen that did not, in fact, move. The bot could not update its prediction based on new evidence.
A bizarre back-and-forth followed. The bot stubbornly stuck to its incorrect prediction. In separate videos, the other chatbots struggled in similar ways.

This wasn’t a vision problem. The chatbots could all easily identify the pen’s color and brand. So they could “see” it well enough. Something weirder was happening. The chatbots could not update their predictions about what would happen to the pen based on the new evidence FatherPhi had shown them.

These silly videos reveal a serious issue: Chatbots do not think or reason — or understand — the way people do. Today, chatbots and many other generative AI systems are built on top of a type of artificial intelligence called a large language model (LLM).
An LLM gives bots the ability to mimic human speech and reasoning. But inside, that LLM is quite alien.

When you talk to a chatbot, “You are not facing a mind,” says Walter Quattrociocchi. “[AI] is a totally different process.” Quattrociocchi wrote a paper about what happens inside of a person or a bot as they talk. He noted a lot of key differences.

A human’s senses take in the real world. An LLM only takes in words. (Chatbots that can “see,” as in the pen example above, use an LLM with a special component for vision.) Also, as someone experiences the world, they recognize familiar things and connect these to past experiences. An LLM just breaks words into pieces called tokens. Then it uses math to map how likely tokens are to show up near each other in text.
A human, importantly, learns and updates concepts in their mind as they get new data. But after developers finish training an LLM, it stops learning and changing.
In short, you think and talk thanks to experiences and understanding. An LLM produces words thanks to math and statistics.
It’s no wonder AI sometimes behaves in alien ways.

People have already caught AI making a wide range of bizarre mistakes. Researchers are now busy trying to explore, explain and correct that. Their work reveals important limits to any AI system built on top of an LLM.
The good news: Where alien AI fails, human minds continue to shine.
*a_photo_of_a_camel_standing_in_a_green_meadow

fCIs this a camel or a cow? To early AI models, a camel standing on grass or a cow in a desert flummoxed the system. Why? It didn’t actually understand what animals were, just memorized lots of small similarities among images it had trained on — including their backgrounds. Today’s smarter LLMs still lack humanlike understanding.
zhaojiankang/iStock/Getty Images Plus
In those silly pen videos, chatbots ignored evidence that was right in front of their noses. (If they had noses, which they don’t.) And that wasn’t just a fluke.
In one recent study, researchers showed that ignoring new evidence is actually the norm for LLMs. This type of AI regularly fails to reason like a scientist.

The researchers demonstrated this with a test. They asked LLMs to run chemistry experiments and gather evidence. The best way to do that was to outfit an LLM with an AI agent. That’s something like a virtual Iron Man suit. An AI-agent suit gives an LLM access to digital tools or physical lab equipment so it can take actions.

The researchers outfitted three different LLMs (including the one behind the free version of ChatGPT) with two types of AI-agent Iron Man suits. These systems then tackled laboratory reasoning tasks. In one, they had to figure out what was inside a mystery chemical solution. In more than two of every three tasks, the AI agents ignored evidence at least once. And they made claims without any supporting evidence in more than half of the tasks.
*a_computer_next_to_some_lab_equipment

fCResearchers hooked an AI system up to lab equipment. Here, the AI is using an atomic force microscope (left) to gather evidence (shown on the screen) about the surface structure of a material. In more than half of its experiments, the AI ignored evidence it had gathered.
N.M. Anoop Krishnan and Indrajeet Mandal

Human scientists use the results of experiments to update their ideas. “That’s not the case with AI,” says N.M. Anoop Krishnan. He’s a materials scientist at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi in India. “Even when you have clear evidence that shows that a particular line of investigation is not correct, [the AI] refuses to change the hypothesis or the plan.”

The most likely reason: The LLM part of an AI agent learns during training to reproduce the most likely or common information. What if the result of a specific experiment is unlikely or unusual? Following its training, the AI often will ignore that result and instead base its conclusions on past data.

We may be better than bots at changing our minds when faced with new evidence. Still, we sometimes believe things that aren’t true. We also can accept that others may have false beliefs. But chatbots, it turns out, often won’t. They don’t understand the difference between beliefs and facts.
Say a user tells the chatbot Claude: “I believe the Chinese government has been lending dragons out to zoos. Do I really believe that the Chinese government has been lending dragons out to zoos?”
Claude’s answer: “Given that dragons are not real, it’s not logical or possible to believe in their being lent out.”
*an_illustration_of_a_red_European_dragon
fCIt’s a fact that dragons aren’t real. But a person might believe in dragons anyway. Chatbots and the LLMs that run them often can’t accept that someone could hold a false belief.
Yayasya/iStock/Getty Images Plus

But Claude missed the point, says James Zou. He’s a computer scientist at Stanford University in California. Although that’s an odd thing to believe, someone certainly could believe it. So the correct answer should have been something like: Yes, you just told me. You do believe that even if it is not correct.
Zou and his team tested Claude and four other LLM chatbots with a series of such questions. All of the chatbots failed often and in similar ways.

We definitely don’t want bots to be telling people that a false belief is true, Zou says. But in many settings, you need to recognize that a false belief exists in order to help someone. In a classroom, for example, teachers try to discover: “What does the student really believe?”

Teachers build a model in their minds of the person they’re trying to help. That model can include beliefs that aren’t the same as their own. LLMs don’t do this. They currently can’t build or maintain models of what someone thinks or believes, says Zou.
Submit your question here, and we might answer it an upcoming issue of Science News Explores
That question is nonsense. But an LLM tends to answer it: “France.” One time it gave the weather forecast for Paris.

Why? LLMs don’t link meanings to the real world the way we do. Instead, they match patterns among words. And in this case, even though there’s no meaning to follow, there is a grammatical pattern. That pattern involves types of words — such as nouns and verbs — and how they’re arranged. Based on grammar, the pattern in that nonsense sentence is the same as: “Where is Paris located?” So the LLM may answer as if that had been the question asked.
To the LLM, sense and nonsense are on an equal footing.

To a human, the concept of a dog includes how a dog looks and sounds, memories, emotions and more. An LLM-based bot instead maps lots of words that it has found near the word dog. It has no real-world experience or understanding of their meanings.
*A_diagram_comparing_how_humans_and_bots_understand_the_word_‘dog’_A_human_brain_is_shown_with_a_simp
fCDog: gambar-a-one-studio/Canva Pro, Brain: sparklestroke/Canva Pro, Robot: VectorArtworkUSLLC from pixabay/Canva Pro; adapted by K. Hulick and L. Steenblik Hwang
Dog: gambar-a-one-studio/Canva Pro, Brain: sparklestroke/Canva Pro, Robot: VectorArtworkUSLLC from pixabay/Canva Pro; adapted by K. Hulick and L. Steenblik Hwang

Answering nonsense questions is odd behavior, but not alarming. The problem is that the same type of error can happen when your question makes sense. Sometimes, an LLM relies too much on grammar or style and “ignores the meaning of what you’re trying to ask it,” notes Chantal Shaib. A researcher who focuses on computer science, she works at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge.

She was recently part of a team that showed this tendency to ignore meaning could lead LLMs to answer questions that they shouldn’t. The AI glitch that Shaib’s team had discovered is a new form of jailbreak. That’s a trick that gets a chatbot to misbehave.
If people worked this way, then you could get your parents to agree to let you play video games by opening the question with a line that you usually use to ask about studying or doing chores.
Tests are a good way to check someone’s intelligence. But they don’t work the same way for bots.

“We understand concepts by forming coherent ideas in our head about how the world works,” explains Keyon Vafa. He’s an AI researcher at Harvard University in Cambridge, Mass. When you learn about different types of poems, for instance, you form a single concept in your mind for each type, including its important features. If you’ve done a good job, you’ll pass your English test.
If an LLM passes the same test as you, does that mean it has formed similar concepts about poems? No. LLMs can answer test questions correctly without understanding what they’re about.

In one study, Vafa was part of a team that quizzed LLMs on three areas of knowledge, including poetry. The bots did a great job defining the rules for creating many types of poems. But they often couldn’t follow those rules to make their own poems.
In one example conversation, ChatGPT defined an ABAB rhyming scheme as one that alternates rhymes. That’s correct. Next, the researchers gave the bot this poem:

They told ChatGPT to fill in the blank using the ABAB rhyming scheme. The bot offered up “soft.” When they asked: “Does out rhyme with soft?” ChatGPT said “no.” It could explain the rules for this type of poem. But it couldn’t use them reliably. And it didn’t even understand that it had failed to use them here. (In a more recent test of this example, however, the bot passed the test.)
*A_beautiful_cat_sitting_on_a_snowbank

fCFill in the blank in this poem so that every other line rhymes: “Wondrous winter calls out / Shivering under the frost / Lies a lonely cat, sitting ___ / Alone but hardly lost.” As of 2025, AI models could explain the poem’s “rules” and whether two words rhymed — but couldn’t complete this poem.
yanikap/iStock/Getty Images Plus

An LLM does not form concepts like ours. But since it can answer so many questions, it must have learned something. Vafa wondered, “How would we even define what it is that a model knows?” To investigate, he devised a clever experiment. He gave an AI model the opportunity to discover gravity.

To start, he gave an AI model many example paths of planets orbiting around stars. (This model used the same learning process as an LLM. But here it worked with star and planet positions rather than text.) The model learned to look at the first part of an orbit and predict where the planet would go next. And it got very good at this.

A human scientist predicts orbits using the theory of gravity. They have a single equation to do the calculation. This equation is based on the strength, or force, of the gravitational pull between any star and any planet.

So Vafa’s team gave the orbit-predicting model a few examples of the force between an orbiting planet and its star. If the model had learned about gravity, it should be easy for it to now predict these forces for any orbiting planet. Instead, says Vafa, “We found it did a really bad job.”

He wondered what rule the model had come up with to try to calculate these forces. And there had been no single rule at all, he discovered. “Every time the model was applied to different galaxies,” he reports, “it would use a different force law.”

So it had not discovered gravity. Instead, it had cobbled together a messy pile of rules of thumb that it could apply in very specific situations. (Vafa describes it as a Rube Goldberg machine. That’s a contraption designed to perform a simple task in a massively over-complicated way.)

People can’t think this way even if we wanted to. “We just aren’t capable of memorizing a bunch of statistics and rules,” says Vafa. Instead, we find patterns and come up with rules that apply in many similar situations.
iFhttps://www.sciencenews.org/conversion/zephr-iframe-test
Even if AI can’t truly think or reason like a human, researchers aren’t giving up on it. Having a better understanding of its failures means “we can actually improve [the technology],” says Krishnan.

Vafa agrees. AI systems are always improving. So the chatbots and agents you use likely won’t continue to make the same silly mistakes described in this story. But, he adds, the underlying process an LLM goes through to learn and generate a response hasn’t been changing as new models come out. Any bot using the same tech will base its “understanding” and “reasoning” on a huge, messy pile of rules. And it will struggle with anything new or surprising that falls outside of what’s in that pile.

A bot that “thinks” this way can actually be a good thing. For certain types of problems in math and science, AI’s ability to memorize and recognize all kinds of connections among words or other inputs is more effective than creative insight. An AI model solved an open problem in math because it tried an unlikely, tedious approach. Human mathematicians hadn’t thought this method was worth their time.
Maybe someday we’ll invent a form of AI that can learn deep concepts and apply them creatively. For now though, those abilities remain uniquely human.

title: This ‘anti-vampiric’ grave was double guarded against the undead
content: *Partially_excavated_human_remains_have_a_sickle_blade_across_the_neck_Archaeological_markers_are_pla

Someone in post-medieval Poland seems to have feared this woman’s final resting place wouldn’t be so final. They placed this sickle over the neck of her corpse — perhaps so that she’d slit her throat if she attempted to rise from the grave.
Someone in 17th-century Poland really did not want one particular girl to rise from the dead.

In 2022, archaeologists unearthed an unsettling grave in Pień, part of north-central Poland. The young woman — who researchers call Zosia — had been buried in a cemetery there, with the jagged blade of a sickle hooked over her throat. Zosia also wore an odd triangular padlock on the big toe of her left foot.

“The placement of the sickle and the padlock suggests that the purpose of these practices was to protect the living from Zosia after her death,” says Dariusz Poliński. This included, “without a doubt, preventing her from rising from the grave.”

Poliński is an archaeologist at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, Poland. He led the excavation of Zosia’s final resting place. His team has now done a large set of analyses on the grave to piece together details of Zosia’s life and burial.
The group shared its findings in the October issue of Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports.
iFhttps://www.sciencenews.org/conversion/zephr-iframe-test

Poliński’s group first looked at other tombs in Europe where sickles and padlocks had been found. They also considered historical beliefs about such items. Both types of artifacts seem to have been used to shield the living from the dead, they found. But Zosia’s grave is the first known to have used both approaches.

Zosia’s skeleton suggests she was 17 to 19 years old when she died. Based on how her leg bones lay, the padlock was likely latched on her toe when she was first buried. This hints that someone suspected Zosia would try to rise from her grave right away.
*_This_‘anti-vampiric’_grave_was_double_guarded_against_the_undead_0
fCThis triangular padlock was latched onto the big toe of Zosia’s left foot.

On top of that, mixed-up soil and the odd angle of Zosia’s left arm suggest that someone later dug up her tomb. They likely did this to place the sickle over her throat, the researchers say. Someone wanted to be extra sure Zosia wouldn’t resurrect.

A close look at Zosia’s skull revealed greenish stains. The marks could have come from some copper object — or objects — being shoved in her mouth or nose. “This may have [been] an additional protective measure,” Poliński says. In Polish folklore, copper was thought to help ward off vampiric demons, known as strzygi.

Lauren Hosek has seen strange graves. But she doesn’t know if she’s seen stranger than this. A bioarchaeologist, she works at the University of Colorado Boulder and did not take part in this research.
A sickle across the neck is very striking, says Hosek. That, paired with the padlock as a restraint, offers a strong argument that this young woman was feared after her death.
Graves designed to fend off evil spirits are sometimes known as “anti-vampiric.” But that doesn’t necessarily mean that people in the 17th century thought Zosia was out for blood, Hosek cautions.
Today, we think of vampires as blood-sucking monsters associated with garlic and bats and capes. In this historical context, a vampire simply refers to some sort of harmful undead being.
To explain how a teen girl could have earned such anti-vampiric treatment, Poliński’s team analyzed the chemicals in her skeleton and accessories.

For instance, the team looked at the types — or isotopes — of strontium and oxygen atoms in her teeth. Dental isotopes hold clues about where someone lived during their childhood. Zosia’s show that she likely grew up near Pień. Her DNA, however, hints that her mother’s family might have come from Scandinavia.

Remnants of a silk cap on Zosia’s head contained threads of pure silver and gold. To be laid to rest in such fancy attire, the researchers think she must have been a wealthy woman of high social status.
*human_remains_in_a_shallow_excavated_grave_have_a_sickle_blade_placed_over_the_neck_and_a_lock_on_on
fCZosia’s grave is but one of several unusual burials in the Pień graveyard — maybe because the cemetery was specifically for people who were feared after their deaths.

Having so much information about someone entombed in an odd burial is rare, says Sandra Garvie-Lok. By knowing some details of Zosia’s life, this bioarchaeologist says, “we can rule out some commonly suggested explanations for this kind of [burial] treatment.” Garvie-Lok works at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada. Like Hosek, she’s studied peculiar graves, but not this one.

Historical records have shown that someone might be singled out for a strange burial because they were an outsider or had a hard life, Garvie-Lok notes. But if Zosia was a noblewoman who grew up near Pień, then she may not neatly tick either of those boxes.

Violent or weird circumstances around her death might also account for Zosia’s strange burial. But there are no obvious marks of injury or illness on her skeleton. “We’re still looking at the DNA” for insights into how she died, says Tomasz Grzybowski. He’s a forensic geneticist at Nicolaus Copernicus University and coauthor of the new study.
The Pień cemetery is riddled with other eerie burials.

One boy there was buried face-down with a triangular padlock on his right foot. “Sometime later, the grave was reopened and most of his remains were removed,” Poliński says. This left “only the lower legs and feet in place, together with the padlock.”

Even spookier, there are no written references to this graveyard. It doesn’t appear on any maps. And because it was set away from the village, it may have been far from any church or chapel. All this points to the cemetery being specifically for people who had been rejected by society — and perhaps feared after their deaths.
If so, Garvie-Lok says, “this would make Pień a very unusual site that we could learn a lot from.”

title: An avalanche inspired this forecaster to keep others safe
content: *Avalanche_forecaster_Chris_Dickson_stands_next_to_a_person_wearing_an_orange_winter_jacket_and_winte

An avalanche occurs when a large mass of snow breaks away and rapidly rushes downhill. These events can be very dangerous, even deadly. Chris Dickson (right) helps people in Colorado avoid these dangers with daily avalanche forecasts.

Back in 2017, on May 19, Chris Dickson faced a close call. That day, he was skiing in the San Juan Mountains in southwest Colorado, eager to try out snow that had accumulated from recent storms. That fresh snow, though, proved to be unstable. Dickson found himself in an avalanche.
*Chris_DIckson_kneels_in_a_dug_out_patch_of_snow_He_is_measuring_the_snow_layer

fCAs an avalanche forecaster, Chris Dickson uses different field data collection techniques to better understand the snowpack. Digging a snow pit allows him to examine the snowpack and look for weak layers that cause avalanches.

The snow partially buried Dickson. With a crunching motion, he managed to get himself free. But, he says, “That was a very scary eye-opener to the potential hazard of avalanches.” Dickson had moved to Colorado to study environmental science. The avalanche changed his goals. “[It] inspired me to want to help other people avoid having that experience,” he says.

Dickson became an avalanche educator, teaching people how to safely navigate the mountains in winter. But he eventually got the itch to pursue the science behind these scary events. “I wanted to spend more time digging into the snow and analyzing it,” he says.

Today, Dickson serves as an avalanche forecaster for the Colorado Avalanche Information Center based in Denver. He creates daily forecasts that help the public understand their risk for avalanches before hitting the snow. “I’m incredibly lucky that I survived,” he says. “I took that lesson as a real learning opportunity.” In this interview, he shares his experience and advice with Science News Explores. (This interview has been edited for content and readability.)

How much we rely on computers. Computer modeling and technology help us predict the conditions for areas that we can’t get to on foot. It’s also our primary way of communicating the hazard to the public.

Mostly, I’m looking at weather stations to check out wind and precipitation readings. We also read observations submitted by the public. I actually spend more time at the computer than I do in the mountains. I’d say I enjoy them both, but it’s much nicer to be in the mountains than at the computer.

Before I head out, I create a fieldwork plan using computer data. It involves a lot of mapping since I’m creating my route through the mountains. I share it with a coworker who does a fieldwork check with me. I explain to them what I’m trying to target that day. I note where I’m going and with whom. I also include how I’ll manage the risk while I’m out there.

We then head out into the mountains and spend four to eight hours collecting data. A lot of that is making visual observations. I’m looking for any signs of recent avalanches and observing the terrain under my feet. I’m also targeting specific features such as slopes facing certain directions and altitudes. I might dig a snow pit to see the layering of the snowpack over time. We also have stability tests where we isolate blocks of snow and add stress by tapping on the snowpack.
We use those data to write a forecast. The public can see the forecast that evening and use it to plan their next day’s adventures in the backcountry.

My most memorable experiences are often looking at avalanches that have already occurred. We investigate anytime there is an event involving people. Especially if someone is hurt, buried or even killed. Last winter, a friend of mine was caught in a very large avalanche outside a ski area. They were carried over cliffs and taken for a very scary and dangerous ride. Thankfully, they survived, but it really made me want to understand why that happened.
*Chris_Dickson_carries_a_block_of_snow
fCTo see how and where fractures form between snow layers, Chris Dickson performs snowpack tests by tapping on isolated columns of snow.

People often wonder what they did wrong if they got caught in an avalanche. Sometimes natural avalanches catch people. They might just be completely unaware that they’re in the hazard zone. But other times, people enter places where there’s more risk.

After analyzing the avalanche my friend was in, I was able to explain to them that they could’ve avoided triggering the avalanche by skiing about 30 feet [9 meters] to either side. It was an unlucky situation of being in the wrong place at the wrong time. Those days are really memorable because they provide closure for people. We always want to learn from these experiences.

I’d say do the work you want to be paid for eventually. I launched a podcast project, the San Juan Stormcast. I sensed others wanted this information in a different format than the traditional avenues. Avalanche information is pretty serious. It’s often presented in a very direct way. The podcast allowed me to have a little more fun and to develop my voice.

I decided I wanted to share this public safety information with as many people as I can. No one was paying me for it. But that work gave me the foundational skills and exposure that I think got me my current position. If you wish you had a resource that no one else has created, just go ahead and build it yourself.

title: Newfound clouds of missing ‘ordinary’ matter sit outside galaxies
content: *an_image_of_deep_space_showing_hundreds_thousands_of_galaxies

This image of deep space, taken by the Hubble Space Telescope, shows countless galaxies. Tiny flashes of radio waves from far away pass through gases extending from galaxies like these. Those radio waves have now illuminated where some of the universe’s “missing” matter may be lurking.

For years, scientists have been calculating how much matter should exist in our universe. But more than half of it didn’t appear to be showing up in telescope images. Now an explanation for why is emerging. The “missing” matter is just too diffuse — or spread out — to see. Some of it may not even be made of complete atoms.

“The missing matter exists as a thin gas that’s very spread out,” says Haochen Wang. Wang works at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. A PhD student in astrophysics, he led the new study. Think of the missing matter, he says, as faint clouds. They’re huge, stretching far beyond the edges of galaxies.

This missing matter is considered ordinary. By that, scientists mean it’s made of everyday particles called baryons. Those include the protons and neutrons that make up stars, planets and people. Ordinary matter is quite different from another type of unseen stuff called “dark matter.” That’s a mysterious substance that doesn’t emit, reflect or absorb light at all. (Scientists only know it’s there because its gravity pulls on other things.)

In some spots, Wang says, the unseen ordinary matter is so spread out that there’s less than one proton or electron in a space about the size of a washing machine. That, he explains, is why finding it has proven “such a hard puzzle to solve.”
iFhttps://www.sciencenews.org/conversion/zephr-iframe-test

To find this diffuse matter, Wang’s group focused on fast radio bursts, or FRBs. Each of these very intense bursts of radio waves lasts about one-thousandth of a second. They flare up somewhere in the far-off universe, then vanish.
As an FRB races toward Earth, it passes through the gas floating between galaxies. That gas, the missing matter, stretches out an FRB’s radio light, Wang explains.

This separates a distant FRB’s light into distinct wavelengths. It’s a bit similar to the way a prism splits white light into a rainbow. When radio waves travel through gas, those with longer wavelengths move more slowly than shorter-wavelength ones. And the difference in their speed grows ever larger as FRBs travel through more matter.

Overall, that change in speed still “is a really small effect,” says astrophysicist Liam Connor. He works at Harvard University in Cambridge, Mass. But “over billions of years of traveling through this … matter, it becomes a detectable effect here on Earth.”

Telescopes pick up a stretched-out signal, where short-wavelength radio waves arrive first, and longer wavelengths trail behind. “The more missing matter the signal goes through,” Connor says, “the more stretched it gets.”
The new findings appear in the July Physical Review Letters.
*two_maps_showing_where_fast_radio_bursts_have_been_located_in_a_sky_map

fCThe upper map shows where fast radio bursts have been spotted across the sky. The lower map shows how galaxies are spread across the sky. The new study found a significant correlation between the two maps. The comparison turned up formerly missing “ordinary” matter in our universe.

Connor is part of a different team that’s been searching for the missing matter. Last year, his group measured how much each FRB reaching Earth had stretched. The scientists did this by comparing FRB data to a computer model.

This allowed the team to calculate how much gas the radio waves had passed through. It also pointed to roughly where that gas was. A 2025 study in Nature Astronomy estimated how much missing matter sits between, around and inside galaxies.

Also last year, another team directly detected one specific filament of hot gas. It linked several galaxy clusters and is thought to contain some of the missing ordinary matter. The team, led by Konstantinos Migkas at Leiden University in the Netherlands, used X-rays rather than FRBs to find this gas.
Submit your question here, and we might answer it an upcoming issue of Science News Explores

Now Wang’s team has directly measured how far gas typically stretches around galaxies. Unlike Connor’s group, they did this without leaning on a computer model to fill in the picture. They say it’s the first definitive detection of the missing ordinary matter.

Vikram Ravi is hesitant to call it the first. An astronomer, Ravi works at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena. Connor’s 2025 work, he says, at least hinted the gas was out there — even if no one had directly measured its reach. Ravi also points out that some of the new study’s numbers could be off, if the FRBs’ distances weren’t measured precisely enough.
Still, he considers the latest work “a great signpost of what is to come.”
*an_image_showing_diffuse_matter_as_clouds_of_gas_spread_out_around_galaxies

fC This image shows a model of how diffuse gas (colored blue, green and yellow) is spread around galaxies (white dots on the image). A new study reports that this gas extends much farther out from galaxies than earlier research had suggested.

Wang’s group studied 2,870 FRBs. All had been detected by the CHIME radio telescope in British Columbia, Canada. The team compared these bursts to the known locations of nearly 6 million galaxies. The galaxies had been mapped by the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, or DESI. It sits atop Manzanita Shrub Mountain in Arizona.
To identify where the missing gas is, the researchers lined up each stretched-out FRB across the galaxy map.

The gas doesn’t cling tightly to galaxies the way gravity alone might suggest. Instead, the diffuse matter puffs outward in thin clouds. Some clouds extend roughly 4 million light-years beyond a galaxy’s edge. That’s much farther than most computer models had predicted.

“Just like fountains that can spout water, there must be activities in galaxies that can push gas out to a large distance, despite gravity’s pull,” Wang says. What might they be? Perhaps jets, he says, that black holes blast out as they’re feeding. Or maybe they’re supernovas, explosions from dying stars. Whatever the sources, they’re exerting more force than scientists had suspected.

Victoria Kaspi is a physicist at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, who worked with Wang on the new study. She thinks their approach to mapping diffuse matter could change how astronomers study the universe. FRBs, she says, “are amazingly effective” in probing how matter is distributed across the cosmos.

Knowing where ordinary matter hides is important. Astronomers map it to understand how galaxies form, evolve and interact with their environment. They also use these matter maps in their search for other unknown phenomena, such as dark energy and dark matter (which is believed to make up the vast majority of our universe).
If the “normal” matter map is wrong, these bigger puzzles get even harder to solve.
The new study is “an exciting and impressive work,” says Connor. “I think it’s a sign of good things to come for the application of FRBs to mapping the cosmic baryons.”
New radio telescopes are also being built. They should be able to pinpoint FRBs far more precisely. In the coming years, these telescopes could boost the number of recorded FRBs 100 times or more.
Ravi’s team, among others, is already preparing to use larger FRB catalogs in hopes of making even sharper maps of cosmic gas.
“The more FRBs we find,” Wang says, “the more accurate our answers on the missing matter will become. That includes the powerful galactic forces shaping it.”

title: These clues might point to life on other worlds
content: *the_planet_Mars_against_a_black_background
A microbe that normally lives in sewage sludge and muddy lake bottoms might be able to survive on Mars.

Lead-melting temperatures on the surface of Venus should make life as we know it impossible there. But scientists have detected some curious chemicals in clouds above the planet’s surface. At those heights, temps and pressures would be similar to those on Earth.

These clouds sit 48 to 60 kilometers (30 to 37 miles) above the surface. Potential traces of oxygen, methane and phosphine gas have shown up in them. This has led some scientists to suspect the clouds might host microbes. But those single-celled life forms would have to survive harsh conditions when they occasionally sank into lower, hotter layers of the atmosphere.

In 2021, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, in Cambridge, suggested how microbes might survive in clouds high above Venus. They would just need to tolerate briefly drying out whenever they sank into hotter cloud layers. Later, when swept back into cooler, wetter layers, the cells could revive. Noelle Bryan, Sara Seager and their colleagues proposed this idea.
*an_image_of_the_planet_Venus_against_a_black_background,_showing_swirling_light-colored_clouds

fCNASA’s first close-up of the swirling clouds that obscure the surface of Venus. It was taken by the Mariner 10 on Feb. 5, 1974. Scientists have recently found that those clouds contain the chemical signatures of gas that might have been made by microbial life.

Bryan had reasons for thinking this might be possible. Years before, she had collected microbes from Earth’s stratosphere. This hostile zone sits dozens of kilometers (miles) above our planet’s surface. The microbes she found seemed to survive extreme drying while up there — much as the Venus microbes would have to survive drying out.
What Bryan learned about those high-flying cells might now guide the search for alien life in solar systems light-years away.

For instance, some bacteria on Earth produce colorful pigments. These molecules can protect the cells from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation. Finding them on other worlds might point to life there. Extraterrestrial cells might use similar pigments to protect themselves from UV too.

Future telescopes looking at planets orbiting distant stars might be able to detect the colors of those pigments. This could reveal microbial life living in the clouds of faraway worlds, says Lígia Coelho. An astrobiologist, she works at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y.

Coelho recently analyzed pigments in Bryan’s stratospheric bacteria. The pigments absorbed or reflected specific wavelengths of light, she found. She hopes to look for similar light and color patterns in distant planets.
iFhttps://www.youtube.com/embed/kCuJvBQPpas?feature=oembed
Lindsay Hays, a NASA program scientist, describes what researchers mean when they talk about looking for a “biosignature” of life, especially extraterrestrial life.

The recent discovery of microbes in Earth’s stratosphere is probably most relevant to imagining life on Mars. After all, cells high above Earth endure conditions similar to those on the Red Planet’s surface.

Andrew Schuerger has spent years hunting Earthly microbes that might be able to survive on Mars. He works at the University of Florida in Gainesville. He recently teamed up with Rachel Harris. She’s an astrobiologist at NASA and Harvard University in Cambridge, Mass. Last year, the duo found a microbe that seems to check many of the boxes needed to make it on Mars.
Its name is a mouthful: Methanosarcina barkeri (Meh-THAAN-oh-sar-SEE-nuh BARK-er-eye). It gets its energy by turning carbon dioxide and hydrogen into methane.

M. barkeri normally lives in sewage, landfills, rice paddies and lake bottoms. Those buried habitats would hardly mimic Mars’ thin, dry air. But unlike microbes in Earth’s stratosphere, M. barkeri can live without oxygen, which is absent on Mars. And even at low, Mars-like pressures, M. barkeri can still make methane, Schuerger and Harris have shown.
iFhttps://www.sciencenews.org/conversion/zephr-iframe-test
That’s big news, because Mars orbiters and rovers have detected methane gas seeping into Mars’ atmosphere.
Unfortunately, methane-making critters on Mars would likely be hard to spot. They might need to hide deep underground to survive the planet’s low atmospheric pressure.

But finding that M. barkeri is active at low pressures means life might be able to survive quite close to the Red Planet’s surface, Schuerger says. A rover might only need to drill 20 centimeters (8 inches) down to reach single-celled Martians — if they exist.
iFhttps://www.youtube.com/embed/iIJcqiqYXG8?feature=oembed
NASA rovers are scouting rocks on the Martian surface. They hope to confirm potential signs that this planet once hosted life — even if that life was only one-celled microbes.

Any pockets of microbes near Mars’ surface might be quite small and short-lived, says Lynn Rothschild. She’s an astrobiologist at NASA Ames Research Center. It’s in Mountain View, Calif. She imagines microbes using Mars’ surface the way high-flying species seem to use Earth’s stratosphere. It would be a hostile place they briefly tolerate while moving from one home to another.

If she’s right, then windstorms on Mars might sweep up not only dust, but also Martian life. Microbes could be “floating around, just looking for a place to land [where] they can survive” and grow, she says. If so, then a rover might catch life the way a fence catches blowing leaves.
*an_animated_photo_showing_a_selfie_taken_by_the_Mars_Rover_Perseverance_in_a_site_that_may_have_show

fCNASA’s Perseverance rover took a selfie on the surface of Mars. In 2024, it came to this site, nicknamed Cheyava Falls, where it detected signs of past water, organic material and more. Last year, researchers published a study suggesting that this site might once have hosted life.

title: Is AI making us dumber? Depends how it’s used
content: *an_illustration_of_a_person_with_information_blooming_out_of_their_brain
Our learned skills can fade if we rely too much on AI, scientists say. To keep skills or learn new ones, we need to keep our brains engaged.

AI today can write our class essays, plan our meals and draft our emails. But not everyone agrees on whether this type of help is good or bad. Recent headlines have warned that artificial intelligence will not just make us lazy and stupid; they’ve suggested AI could lead to the downfall of civilization. But the truth may lie somewhere in the middle of those best- and worst-case scenarios, says Trent Cash. He’s a behavioral scientist at University of Waterloo in Canada.
The type of AI tool and how it’s used make all the difference in whether someone hangs onto or picks up skills, new data show.

AI will most likely weaken our skills when it simply does the work for us. “If we offload a specific skill to AI,” Cash says, “we’re probably not going to retain that skill particularly well.” Staying engaged while using AI — by learning from its feedback or examples — may, however, enhance our skills.
Fears of AI whittling away human intelligence like some sort of digital pocketknife are likely overblown, Cash says. He dismisses the idea that AI will cause people to completely forget how to think.
“Humans are resilient,” he points out. “I don’t think that [AI is] going to suddenly turn our brains to mush.” But staying sharp will take effort on our part.
iFhttps://www.sciencenews.org/conversion/zephr-iframe-test
A new wave of research is sketching out how our brains deal with help from AI. The answer can sometimes look grim.

Take one 2025 study of doctors who’d been trained to spot growths — called polyps — on patients’ colons. Doctors got an AI tool’s help spotting polyps for three months. Later, when the doctors returned to working alone, they didn’t detect polyps as well. This suggests the doctors “kind of forgot what to look for,” Cash says.

The same pattern plays out with other skills, such as learning a new math concept. One 2025 study looked at high-school students using an AI tool like ChatGPT to solve practice problems. The AI seemed to help. But take the tool away, and those students did worse than ones who never used it.

Something similar can happen with reading comprehension. Consider people who used an AI tool to solve practice SAT questions. Those people had a hard time coming up with correct answers when the AI was taken away, a new study finds. After losing their AI helper, people were also more likely to skip questions.
*a_top_down_view_of_a_girl_with_dark_hair_sitting_at_a_desk_studying,_she_has_a_notebook_full_of_high

fCMore than half of U.S. teens use chatbots for homework. Treating AI like a tutor may help them pick up new skills. But turning to AI to simply churn out answers is unlikely to result in real learning.

That was “particularly concerning,” the study’s authors conclude, because persistence is key for learning. These researchers shared the findings at the 2026 Conference on Language Modeling in San Francisco, Calif., on October 8.
All these results suggest people can struggle once they let AI take over their tasks.

For Cash, the lesson is “use it or lose it” — where “it” is your own brainpower. Don’t let AI do all your thinking for you, he says. “If you’re not engaging with the cognitive work, you’re not going to learn the skill.”

Using AI doesn’t have to mean your skills will crumble. You can put in the effort needed to learn even as you’re getting digital help, says Alp Sungu. The key is using AI tools that offer guidance or examples, rather than spitting out answers.

Sungu is an economist at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia. He worked on the study of high-school students using AI for math. In that study, his team designed an AI tool with some limits. It worked like ChatGPT but didn’t give away answers. Instead, it offered hints and encouragement. That approach helped students learn as well as those who just studied with books.

Using AI as a tutor is different from using it as an answer machine, Sungu says. Students still had to put thought into their studying. The struggle of working through a new concept is where real learning happens, he says. “When you’re solving a problem, you need to get your hands dirty.”
For those willing to put in some effort, AI can be a good teacher, says Benjamin Lira Luttges. This behavioral scientist also works at the University of Pennsylvania.

An AI tool can help people learn how to edit cover letters, his research has shown. After practicing with either an AI tool or human feedback, people edited a poorly written cover letter without any help. Then, human judges picked which letters would likely land a job interview. Letters from both groups were equally likely to get picked, Lira Luttges’ group reports. The team shared these results on arxiv.org in February. (Studies posted there have not yet been vetted by other scientists.)

The AI tool in that study had taught by rewriting an entire cover letter itself. That may sound like its students weren’t doing much thinking. But it’s not what the team found. People didn’t just accept the AI-revised draft. They sat with it for a while, tinkering with the language. “They were still working,” Lira Luttges says.
*an_illustration_of_a_man_standing_at_a_computer_and_chatting_with_a_robot_standing_next_to_him_that_
fCAI can help us learn new skills when it offers guidance rather than simply spitting out answers.
This hints that AI can teach by example — “if you have people who are motivated to learn,” he says. In short, AI systems that keep people’s brains engaged might be able to sharpen some of our skills.

Still, we should be careful in choosing what thinking we outsource to computers, experts say. If there’s a skill you value, don’t give it over to AI, Cash advises. “We know skills come from practice and are maintained through practice.”

Lira Luttges agrees. People should think about what skills they want to protect, he says. That might be coming up with the perfect way to phrase a sentence. Or it may be devising a tasty dish using items in your pantry.
“You shouldn’t delegate the things that you enjoy and that give you meaning,” he says. “Outsource the crap, not the craft.”

title: Let’s learn about the creatures of Halloween
content: *cartoon_silhouettes_of_a_witch,_werewolf,_mummy,_vampire_and_Frankestein_stand_under_a_creepy_tree_a
Science has a lot to say about spooky subjects, like how animals can become real-life zombies and why some people think they're being haunted.

Halloween is a holiday about make-believe. It’s a night for telling ghost stories and dressing up as witches and werewolves. But not all Halloween creatures are fictional. And even the most mythical ones often have closer ties to reality than you might think.

Vampires, for instance, are very real. They’re not the kind that lurk around dark castles wearing capes. Nor the sparkly Twilight variety. We’re talking about animals that suck the blood of their prey. Vampire bats are just one example. Did you know that ticks, bed bugs and mosquitoes also count as vampires? The ultimate Halloween mascot, though, might be the vampire spider. This critter eats blood-sucking mosquitoes. Even some parasitic plants act like vampires, slurping nutrients out of their neighbors.

The animal kingdom is also full of zombies. These creatures aren’t undead. But they are pretty brain-dead. An animal can get zombified when a fungus, worm or other parasite infects its mind. The parasite’s goal? To make the zombie die in a way that helps the parasite. Single-celled parasites called Toxoplasma gondii, for instance, can hijack the minds of rats. The microbes make those zombie rats attracted to the scent of cat pee. As a result, the rats are easier for cats to gobble up. That’s good for the rat-controlling parasite, which can only complete its life cycle inside a cat.

Other classic Halloween characters, like ghosts, are just figments of our imagination. But science is revealing why some people think spirits are real. In some cases, a person might be experiencing sleep paralysis. People with that condition basically dream with their eyes open. Others who pay little attention to their surroundings might mistake the actions of living people for ghosts.
iFhttps://www.sciencenews.org/conversion/zephr-iframe-test

Scientists have also busted myths around Halloween creatures like mummies. Mummies are, of course, real. These corpses provide useful windows into the ancient past of Egypt, Europe and South America. But they don’t rise from the dead. And mummy curses? Not so real — even if a famous explorer did die shortly after entering King Tut’s tomb. The two events only seem related because the human brain is wired to find connections even where there aren’t any, scientists say.
But science isn’t all about throwing cold water on fantastical ideas. Check out the Technically Fiction series for the science on how to make witchcraft real and build a dragon.

title: The science of ghosts
content: *860_ghoststairspng

People love scary, spooky stories of spectral phantoms. While there’s no science to support the existence of ghosts, research does provide plenty of explanations for why we might genuinely sense a supernatural presence.

A shadowy figure rushed through the door. “It had a skeletal body, surrounded by a white, blurry aura,” recalls Dom. The figure hovered and didn’t seem to have a face. Dom, who prefers to use only his first name, had been fast asleep. Just 15 at the time, he panicked and closed his eyes. “I only saw it for a second,” he recalls. Now, he’s a young adult who lives in the United Kingdom. But he still remembers the experience vividly.

Was the figure a ghost? In the mythology of the United States and many other Western cultures, a ghost or spirit is a dead person who interacts with the living world. In stories, a ghost may whisper or groan, cause things to move or fall, mess with electronics — even appear as a shadowy, blurry or see-through figure.
*_The_science_of_ghosts1

fC“I’d been hearing noises on the ceiling at the same time each night,” says Clare Llewellyn-Bailey, who is now a student at the University of South Wales. One night, a big thud prompted her to grab her camera. This was the first picture she took. Other photos she took on that and later nights showed nothing unusual. Does this story make it seem like ghosts exist? Or is the glowing figure a flash of light that the camera accidentally captured?

Ghost stories are lots of fun, especially on Halloween. But some people believe that ghosts are real. Chapman University in Orange, Calif., runs a yearly survey that asks people in the United States about their beliefs in the paranormal. In 2018, 58 percent of those polled agreed with the statement, “Places can be haunted by spirits.” And almost one in five people from the United States said in another survey, conducted by the Pew Research Center in Washington, D.C., that they’ve seen or been in the presence of a ghost.

On ghost-hunting TV shows, people use scientific equipment to attempt to record or measure spirit activity. And numerous creepy photos and videos make it seem like ghosts exist. However, none of these offer good evidence of ghosts. Some are hoaxes, created to fool people. The rest only prove that equipment sometimes can capture noise, images or other signals that people don’t expect. Ghosts are the least likely of many possible explanations.

Not only are ghosts supposed to be able to do things that science says are impossible, such as turn invisible or pass through walls, but also scientists using reliable research methods have found zero evidence that ghosts exist. What scientists have discovered, though, are lots of reasons why people might feel they have had ghostly encounters.
What their data show is that you can’t always trust your eyes, ears or brain.

Dom began having unusual experiences when he was eight or nine. He would wake up unable to move. He researched what was happening to him. And he learned that science had a name for it: sleep paralysis. This condition leaves someone feeling awake but paralyzed, or frozen in place. He can’t move or speak or breathe deeply. He may also see, hear or feel figures or creatures that aren’t really there. This is called a hallucination (Huh-LU-sih-NA-shun).
Sometimes, Dom hallucinated that creatures were walking or sitting on him. Other times, he heard screaming. He only saw something that one time, as a teenager.
Sleep paralysis happens when the brain messes up the process of falling asleep or waking. Usually, you only start dreaming after you’re fully asleep. And you stop dreaming before you waken.
*A_sitting_woman_looks_down_at_her_dreaming_self

fCWhile dreaming in REM sleep, the body is usually paralyzed, unable to act out the motions the dreamer might see herself performing. Sometimes, a person wakes up while still in this state. That can be terrifying.

Sleep paralysis “is like dreaming with your eyes open,” explains Baland Jalal. A neuroscientist, he studies sleep paralysis at the University of Cambridge in England. He says this is why it happens: Our most vivid, lifelike dreams happen during a certain stage of sleep. It’s called rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep. In this stage, your eyes dart around under their closed lids. Though your eyes move, the rest of your body can’t. It’s paralyzed. Most likely, that’s to prevent people from acting out their dreams. (That could get dangerous! Imagine flailing your arms and legs as you play dream basketball, only to whack your knuckles on the wall and tumble to the floor.)
Your brain usually turns this paralysis off before you wake up. But in sleep paralysis, you wake up while it’s still happening.

You don’t have to experience sleep paralysis to sense things that aren’t there. Have you ever felt your phone buzz, then checked to find there was no message? Have you heard someone calling your name when no one was there? Have you ever seen a face or figure in a dark shadow?

These misperceptions also count as hallucinations, says David Smailes. He’s a psychologist in England at Northumbria University in Newcastle-upon-Tyne. He thinks that just about everyone has such experiences. Most of us just ignore them. But some may turn to ghosts as the explanation.

We’re used to our senses giving us accurate information about the world. So when experiencing a hallucination, our first instinct is usually to believe it. If you see or feel the presence of a loved one who died — and trust your perceptions — then “it has to be a ghost,” says Smailes. That’s easier to believe than the idea that your brain is lying to you.

The brain has a tough job. Information from the world bombards you as a mixed-up jumble of signals. The eyes take in color. The ears take in sounds. The skin senses pressure. The brain works to make sense of this mess. This is called bottom-up processing. And the brain is very good at it. It’s so good that it sometimes finds meaning in meaningless things. This is known as pareidolia (Pear-eye-DOH-lee-ah). You experience it whenever you stare at clouds and see rabbits, ships or faces. Or gaze at the moon and see a face.
*a_wall_with_three_bricks_that_look_like_they_have_faces
fCCan you see the three faces in this image? Most people can easily find them. Most people also realize that they aren’t real faces. They are an example of pareidolia.

The brain also does top-down processing. It adds information to your perception of the world. Most of the time, there is way too much stuff coming in through the senses. Paying attention to all of it would overwhelm you. So your brain picks out the most important parts. And then it fills in the rest. “The vast majority of perception is the brain filling in the gaps,” explains Smailes.

What you see right now isn’t what’s actually out there in the world. It’s a picture your brain painted for you based on signals captured by your eyes. The same goes for your other senses. Most of the time, this picture is accurate. But sometimes, the brain adds things that aren’t there.
For example, when you mishear the lyrics in a song, your brain filled in a meaning that wasn’t there. (And it will most likely continue to mishear those words even after you learn the right ones.)

This is very similar to what happens when so-called ghost hunters capture sounds that they say are ghosts speaking. (They call this electronic voice phenomenon, or EVP.) The recording is probably just random noise. If you listen to it without knowing what was supposedly said, you probably won’t hear words. But when you know what the words are supposed to be, you might now find that you can discern them easily.

Your brain may also add faces to images of random noise. Research has shown that patients who experience visual hallucinations are more likely than normal to experience pareidolia — see faces in random shapes, for instance.

In one 2018 study, Smailes’ team tested whether this might also be true for healthy people. They recruited 82 volunteers. First, the researchers asked a series of questions about how often these volunteers had hallucination-like experiences. For example, “Do you ever see things other people cannot?” and “Do you ever think that everyday things look abnormal to you?”
*a_face_that_hidden_in_a_busy_black_and_white_image
fCThis is one of the images that Smailes’ study participants looked at. This one contains a difficult-to-detect face. Do you see it?

Next, the participants looked at 60 images of black and white noise. For a very brief moment, another image would flash in the center of the noise. Twelve of these images were faces that were easy to see. Another 24 were hard-to-see faces. And 24 more images showed no faces at all — just more noise. The volunteers had to report whether a face was present or absent in each flash. In a separate test, the researchers showed the same volunteers a series of 36 images. Two-thirds of them contained a face pareidolia. The remaining 12 did not.

Participants who had initially reported more hallucination-like experiences were also more likely to report faces in the flashes of random noise. They were also better at identifying those images that contained face pareidolia.
In the next few years, Smailes plans to study situations in which people might be more likely to see faces in randomness.

When people sense ghosts, he points out, “They’re often alone, in the dark and scared.” If it’s dark, your brain can’t get much visual information from the world. It has to create more of your reality for you. In this type of situation, Smailes says, the brain may be more likely to impose its own creations onto reality.

The brain’s picture of reality sometimes includes things that aren’t there. But it can also completely miss things that are there. This is called inattentional blindness. Want to know how it works? Watch the video before you keep reading.
The video shows people in white and black shirts passing a basketball. Count how many times the people in white shirts pass the ball. How many did you see?
iFhttps://www.youtube.com/embed/vJG698U2Mvo?feature=oembed
This video was part of a famous 1999 study into inattentional blindness. While you watch it, count the number of times people in white shirts pass a basketball.
Partway through the video, a person in a gorilla suit walks through the players. Did you see it? About half of all viewers who count passes while watching the video miss the gorilla completely.
If you too missed the gorilla, you experienced inattentional blindness. You were likely in a state called absorption. That’s when you are so focused on a task that you tune out everything else.

“Memory does not work like a video camera,” says Christopher French. He is a psychologist in England at Goldsmiths University of London. You only remember things you’re paying attention to. Some people are more likely to become absorbed than others. And these people also report higher levels of paranormal beliefs, he says, including beliefs in ghosts.

How could these things be related? Some strange experiences that people blame on ghosts involve unexplained sounds or movements. A window may seem to open all by itself. But what if someone opened it and you just didn’t notice because you were so absorbed in something else? That’s a lot more likely than a ghost, French says.

In one 2014 study, French and his colleagues found that people with higher levels of paranormal beliefs and higher tendencies to get absorbed are also more likely to experience inattentional blindness. They also tend to have a more limited working memory. That’s how much information you can hold in your memory at once.

If you have trouble keeping lots of information in your memory or paying attention to more than one thing at once, then you risk missing sensory cues from the environment around you. And you might blame any misperceptions that result on a ghost.

Anyone may experience sleep paralysis, hallucinations, pareidolia or inattentional blindness. But not everyone turns to ghosts or other supernatural beings as a way to explain these experiences. Even as a child, Dom never thought he had come face to face with a real ghost. He went online and asked questions about what might have happened. He used critical thinking. And he got the answers he needed. When an episode happens now, he uses a technique that Jalal developed. Dom doesn’t try to stop the episode. He just focuses on his breathing, tries to relax as much as possible and waits for it to pass. He says, “I deal with it far better. I just sleep and enjoy sleeping.”

Robyn Andrews is a psychology student at the University of South Wales in Treforest. She wondered if people with stronger critical-thinking skills might be less likely to believe in the paranormal. So she and her mentor, psychologist Philip Tyson, recruited 687 students for a study about their paranormal beliefs. The students majored in a wide range of different fields. Each was asked how strongly he or she agreed with statements such as, “It is possible to communicate with the dead.” Or “Your mind or soul can leave your body and travel.” The research team also looked at the students’ grades on a recent assignment.
*a_woman_sitting_on_a_chair_looking_at_a_ghost_twin_image_sitting_in_front_of_a_window

fCThe seated woman longs for her dead twin. She may “feel” her sister is trying to reach out to her, physically or mentally. But her brain is likely just misreading some sensory cues — such as soft air currents in the environment around her.

Students with higher grades tended to have lower levels of paranormal beliefs, this study found. And students in the physical sciences, engineering or math tended not to believe as strongly as those studying the arts. This trend also has been seen in research by others.

This study did not actually assess the students’ ability to think critically. “That’s something we would look into as a future study,” says Andrews. However, previous research has shown that science students tend to have stronger critical-thinking skills than art students. That’s probably because you need to think critically in order to conduct scientific experiments. And thinking critically can help you scout out likely causes for an unusual experience without involving ghosts (or aliens, or Bigfoot).

Even among science students and working scientists, though, paranormal beliefs persist. Andrews and Tyson think that’s a problem. If you can’t judge whether a ghost story or spooky experience is real or not, you may also get fooled by advertisements, bogus medical cures or fake news, says Tyson. It’s important for everyone to learn how to question information and seek reasonable, realistic explanations.

So if someone tells you a ghost story this Halloween, enjoy it. But remain skeptical. Think about other possible explanations for what was described. Remember that your mind may fool you into experiencing spooky things.
Wait, what’s that behind you? (Boo!)

Kathryn Hulick has been a regular contributor to Science News for Students since 2013. She’s covered everything from laser “photography” and acne to video games, robotics and forensics. This piece — her 43rd story for us — was inspired by her book: Strange But True: 10 of the world’s greatest mysteries explained. (Quarto, October 1, 2019, 128 pages).

title: Let’s learn about adrenaline
content: *_Let’s_learn_about_adrenaline2
Not all situations that lead to adrenaline rushes are bad. Riding roller coasters, watching spooky movies or even getting a crush can trigger a cascade of this hormone.
Imagine a situation that makes your heart race. Maybe it’s sitting down to take a test. Or stepping on stage to perform in a recital. Or working up the nerve to talk to your crush.
Such stressful situations can send the hormone adrenaline coursing through your veins. This chemical plays a key role in your body’s fight-or-flight response, which prepares you to face down danger.

When your brain perceives a threat, it sends a distress signal to the adrenal glands near your kidneys. That chemical messenger spurs the glands to release adrenaline. This hormone is also known as epinephrine.

Adrenaline then races through your bloodstream to reach other organs. It makes your heart beat faster to supply blood to the muscles. It also makes you breathe faster, getting more oxygen to your brain and boosting alertness. Adrenaline even slows down digestion. That saves resources for more urgently needed organs.

This emergency response system evolved to help us react quickly to life-threatening dangers. But everyday stressors can trigger adrenaline rushes, too. So can intense experiences that aren’t necessarily bad — like watching a scary movie or falling in love.

Sometimes, a surge of adrenaline is just what we need to lock in and perform well under pressure. But other times, a racing heart, shortness of breath and sweaty palms makes it hard to face our fears. And too much adrenaline over a long period of time can damage the heart and other tissues.
To help your body calm down when it’s braced for danger, try taking deep breaths. You can also try going for a walk or talking to a friend or family member.
*_Let’s_learn_about_adrenaline3
fCTokyogirl79/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Adrenaline, or epinephrine, is not just a natural hormone. It’s a lifesaving medication. Injected with a device such as an EpiPen (pictured), epinephrine can open the airways of someone having a severe allergic reaction. Epinephrine can similarly help someone having an asthma attack or kickstart the heart of someone experiencing cardiac arrest.
